audits.area: README.md quantitative claim tracing — every stated number re-derived against its artefact or code

findings.title: "45 fabricated residues" is inflated by a cross-target attribution defect: at least 17 of the 45 are residues the project's own audit calls correct, or artefacts of a 2-character alias matching "TM1"
findings.location: platform/validate.py:181-203 (check_residues alias loop); claimed at README.md:254 and README.md:560
findings.reproduction: cd /Users/seunghojung/Documents/DeepMind_Bio && ./.venv/bin/python platform/validate.py --json > /tmp/gate_live.json; then a script that, for each fabricated_residue failure, splits the source bindingSites string on ';' and '&' and asks whether the flagged target is named in the same clause as the residue token, and separately cross-references data/residue_audit.json['verified_correct'].
findings.observed:
45 fabricated_residue failures, 37 distinct (target,residue) pairs.
"fabricated_residue failures where the target is NOT named in that clause (spurious cross-attribution): 14", e.g.
  SPURIOUS: HippoDual-TrkB-AMPK-X5  Lys45  -> NTRK2  clause='AMPK α-subunit kinase domain (Lys45, Arg67)'
  SPURIOUS: PfcDual-nACh-GluN2A-P5  Tyr188 -> GRIN2A clause='α7 nAChR ECD (Tyr188)'
  SPURIOUS: Curcumin (Curcuma longa) Asp32  -> KEAP1  clause='BACE1 Asp32, Asp228'
  SPURIOUS: Asiatic Acid            Tyr334 -> NTRK2  clause='Keap1 Tyr334, Arg415'
Cross-reference against the project's own audit returned 8 hits:
  'Tyr188 flagged for GRIN2A but audit says CORRECT for [CHRNA7]'
  'Tyr334 / Arg415 flagged for NTRK2 but audit says CORRECT for [KEAP1]'
  'Lys28 / Asp23 flagged for ACHE and for KEAP1 but audit says CORRECT for [APP]'
  'Phe174 flagged for CHRM1 but audit says CORRECT for [PTAFR]'
Additionally, 4 CHRM1 attributions fire on a string with no standalone 'M1' token: "CHRM1 attributions with NO standalone 'M1' token: 4", all from Ginkgolide B's site string 'PAFR His14 (TM1), Tyr200 (TM5), Phe174 (TM3); GABA_A Thr261 (TM2)' — the CHRM1 alias "M1" matches the substring "TM1" (transmembrane helix 1).
findings.why_wrong: check_residues iterates over every target whose alias appears anywhere in the binding-site string and then checks EVERY residue token in that string against EVERY matched target. For any record naming two proteins, residues correct for protein A are re-checked against protein B, fail there, and are counted as "wrong under every convention" residue-identity errors. The alias test is a bare case-insensitive substring match, so the 2-character CHRM1 alias "M1" matches "TM1"/"TM10" etc. The README states the number as "45 residue identities that are wrong in every convention" — that is a claim about residue identity, and ≥17 of the 45 are not. The count also silently reclassifies Trp84/Tyr121 (which README itself explains, correctly, as Torpedo numbering) as identity errors, with the gate emitting "this is a residue-identity error, not a numbering-convention one" for exactly the residues README's own Slate #4 table calls a numbering problem.
findings.fix: In platform/validate.py check_residues, scope residue tokens to the clause that names the target: split the site string on [;&] (and on ',' where a new protein name appears), and only check tokens inside a segment whose text contains the target alias. Require word-boundary alias matching (re.search(rf'(?<![A-Za-z0-9]){re.escape(alias)}(?![A-Za-z0-9])', seg)) so "M1" cannot match "TM1". Add a REVIEWED_TARGETS allow-list so residues belonging to proteins not in the registry (Aβ/APP, BACE1, GABA_A, AMPK) are reported as unresolvable rather than fabricated. Then re-run and republish the corrected count in README.md:254/:560, the badge, and verify_all.py's blurb; add a regression test asserting that Tyr334 in 'Keap1 Tyr334, Arg415' is never attributed to NTRK2.

findings.title: README states the 1000 Da ADMET rule was "deleted"; it is still in the code and is the first refusal reason emitted
findings.reproduction: cd /Users/seunghojung/Documents/DeepMind_Bio && ./.venv/bin/python -c "import sys,json; sys.path.insert(0,'platform'); from cbc.compute import admet; from rdkit import Chem; print('AD_MAX_MW =', admet.AD_MAX_MW); v=admet.check_applicability(Chem.MolToSmiles(Chem.MolFromSequence(json.load(open('data/extracted_raw.json'))['FULL_BRAIN_DRUGS_DATA'][7]['sequence']))); [print(' REASON:',r) for r in v.reasons]"  (run in the audit as a short script over the heaviest valid candidate)
findings.observed:
AD_MAX_MW = 1000.0
heaviest peptide candidate: PfcGluN2A-LTP-P3  MW 5436.2 Da  len 45
in_domain: False
  REASON: molecular weight 5436 Da exceeds 1000 Da. TDC ADMET training sets are drug-like small molecules; nothing of this size is represented.
  REASON: 378 heavy atoms exceeds 70
  REASON: peptide backbone detected (45 amide bonds, 5436 Da). ...
findings.why_wrong: README's "Applicability domain" section is built on the assertion that the 1000 Da rule was removed because it failed the "stated ground must be the computed ground" test, and that the refusal now survives only on the 2285.7 Da heaviest-covalent-species ground. The rule is present, active, and fires first, carrying the exact wording the README says was disqualifying ("nothing of this size is represented") — a sentence that is also directly contradicted by README's own claim that the training bounding box reaches 5299.5 Da. This is a public claim about the state of the code that grep and execution both refute. Separately, the framing selects a 4910 Da candidate to argue MW is not the disqualifier, but no candidate weighs 4910 Da (nearest computed: 4903.6 Da PfcACh-PAM-P1; heaviest 5436.2 Da PfcGluN2A-LTP-P3), and 5436.2 Da is outside the quoted 5299.5 Da box — so the stated argument does not hold for the actual heaviest query.
findings.fix: Either delete AD_MAX_MW/its reason string from platform/cbc/compute/admet.py and let the peptide-backbone and heavy-atom grounds carry the refusal, or amend README.md:499-503 to say the rule was demoted rather than deleted and re-derive the argument against the actual heaviest candidate (5436.2 Da). Add a test asserting that no refusal reason cites a bound the project has retracted.

findings.title: Public repository with no LICENSE file, a "private research" licence line, and committed ChEMBL/UniProt content under a source-file claim that "nothing is redistributed"
findings.location: README.md:12 and README.md:569-571; platform/cbc/corpus.py:12-14; data/corpus_ACHE.json; data/study_ache_affinity.json; data/study_affinity_corrected.json; data/target_registry.json
findings.reproduction: cd /Users/seunghojung/Documents/DeepMind_Bio && ls -la | grep -i licen ; sed -n '12p;569,571p' README.md ; sed -n '12,14p' platform/cbc/corpus.py ; ./.venv/bin/python -c "import json; d=json.load(open('data/corpus_ACHE.json')); print('%d ChEMBL compounds, %d ChEMBL activity measurements, %d canonical_smiles' % (len(d['compounds']), sum(len(c['activities']) for c in d['compounds']), sum(1 for c in d['compounds'] if c.get('canonical_smiles')))); t=json.load(open('data/target_registry.json'))['targets']; print('%d UniProt entries, %d aa of sequence' % (len(t), sum(len(v['sequence']) for v in t.values())))"
findings.observed:
`ls | grep -i licen` returns nothing — there is no LICENSE file in the repository root.
README.md:12 badge: license-private_research; README.md:571: "Private research."
platform/cbc/corpus.py:12-14: "Sources are queried live; nothing is redistributed. ChEMBL data is CC BY-SA 3.0 and COCONUT is CC0/CC BY, but this module stores only identifiers plus locally computed values..."
But: "data/corpus_ACHE.json: 18 ChEMBL compounds, 27 ChEMBL activity measurements, 18 canonical_smiles" and "data/target_registry.json: 16 UniProt entries with full sequences, total 11673 aa". Committed rows in data/study_ache_affinity.json (17) and data/study_affinity_corrected.json (15) each carry chembl id + smiles + measured potency. `grep -in "CC BY|CC-BY|Creative Commons|attribution" README.md` returns no licence/attribution section.
findings.why_wrong: Three distinct exposures now that the repo is public. (1) No LICENSE file means no grant to anyone; "private research" on a public repo is a contradiction that leaves downstream users with no defined rights. (2) corpus.py's in-code assertion that "nothing is redistributed" and that only "identifiers plus locally computed values" are stored is false: canonical_smiles, compound names, and 27 ChEMBL-measured activity values (activity_type, value_nm, assay_chembl_id, document) are ChEMBL's curated content, committed to git. ChEMBL is CC BY-SA 3.0, which requires both attribution and share-alike on redistribution — share-alike is incompatible with an all-rights-reserved public repo. (3) 11,673 aa of UniProt sequence (CC BY 4.0, attribution required) and 16 PDB-derived receptor/peptide sequences are redistributed with no attribution statement anywhere in README.
findings.fix: Add a LICENSE file that actually matches intent and resolve the CC BY-SA conflict — either license the repo (and at minimum data/corpus_ACHE.json and the ChEMBL-derived study rows) under CC BY-SA 3.0-compatible terms, or strip the redistributed ChEMBL values back to identifiers only and regenerate those files from a live query at run time. Correct platform/cbc/corpus.py:12-14 to state what is actually committed. Add a "Data sources and attribution" section to README crediting ChEMBL (CC BY-SA 3.0), UniProt (CC BY 4.0), the PDB (CC0) and Boltz-2 (MIT). Replace the "private research" badge and licence line.

(live counts also give mixed_numbering_convention 2, the committed artefact 3; the committed artefact's fabricated_residue detail strings are in the pre-registry message format, confirming it predates the current code path.)
findings.why_wrong: The first thing a visitor to a public repo sees is the badge row, and the Data-gate badge states a number the linked tool contradicts by 33 violations — a number README's own body text (line 255) identifies as the *superseded* figure. Update the README badge to the live figure (and re-derive that figure after RI-01 is fixed). Add a CI check asserting that data/validation_gate.json matches a fresh run.

findings.title: "paired t-test p = 0.978" is the Holm-adjusted p; the paired t-test itself gives 0.489
findings.location: README.md:229 (Slate #2, MSA paragraph); source values in data/study_inference_variance_analysis.json
findings.reproduction: cd /Users/seunghojung/Documents/DeepMind_Bio && ./.venv/bin/python -c "import json; from scipy import stats; a=json.load(open('data/study_inference_variance_analysis.json')); print('p_raw ', a['p_raw']); print('p_holm', a['p_holm']); mp=a['msa_paired']; t,p=stats.ttest_rel([x['with'] for x in mp],[x['without'] for x in mp]); print('re-derived paired t two-sided p = %.5f' % p)"
findings.why_wrong: README names the test and attaches a number that is not that test's output. The paired t-test across the six candidates gives p = 0.489 (I reproduced it to five decimals from the stored msa_paired array). 0.978 is that value after Holm correction over three hypotheses (0.48925 × 2 = 0.9785). Because the claim is an acceptance of a null ("MSA is immaterial"), the mislabel runs in the flattering direction: a reader takes p = 0.978 as much stronger agreement with the null than p = 0.489 warrants. The same mislabel is propagated into memory/ledger/study-inference-variance.jsonl and memory/views/claims.md:1448, where the claim cites data/study_inference_variance_analysis.json as its source — the artefact that stores 0.489.
findings.fix: Change README.md:229 to "paired t-test p = 0.489 (Holm-adjusted across the three hypotheses, 0.978)", and correct the corresponding ledger claim text. A p-value should never be printed under a test's name unless it is that test's raw output; adopt the convention used elsewhere in the repo (Slate #1 correctly writes "Holm p = 0.814").

audits.verdict:
The README's scientific numbers are, overwhelmingly, real. I traced roughly 90 quantitative claims to artefacts and re-derived them; the great majority match to the digit, and several I recomputed independently from raw rows rather than reading stored summaries (Spearman rho 0.8471/p 3.47e-05 in Slate #7, the paired t-test p 0.7681 and dz 0.1271 in Slate #10, the pooled across-seed SD 2.6615 in Slate #2, the 8/8 and 17/17 registry confirmations, and all 8 pre-registration SHA-256 hashes). The pre-registration machinery, the noise-floor qualification of the headline overstatement finding, and the null-controlled candidate screen are sound work that says what the data says, including where the data refutes the author's own hypotheses.

Three things must be fixed before this README stands as a public scientific claim.

First, "45 fabricated residues" is wrong as stated, and it is wrong in the project's most sensitive register. platform/validate.py checks every residue token against every target named anywhere in the same string, so residues correct for one protein are counted as fabricated for another: at minimum 14 attributions place a residue against a target not named in its own clause, 8 of them contradicting the project's own data/residue_audit.json verified_correct list (Keap1's Tyr334/Arg415 counted as fabricated NTRK2 residues; CHRNA7's Tyr188 as a fabricated GRIN2A residue), and 4 more come from the two-character CHRM1 alias "M1" matching the substring "TM1". The defensible number is materially smaller than 45, and the count also reclassifies the Torpedo-numbered Trp84/Tyr121 as identity errors, contradicting README's own Slate #4 table.

Second, the "Applicability domain" section asserts that the 1000 Da ADMET rule was deleted. It is at platform/cbc/compute/admet.py:56 and fires as the first refusal reason, carrying the exact sentence README says disqualified it. That section is the README's showcase for "the stated ground must be the computed ground," which makes the discrepancy more than clerical.

Third, the repository went public with no LICENSE file, a "private research" licence line, and committed ChEMBL measured activities (27 values, plus SMILES and names) and 11,673 aa of UniProt sequence, under a source-file comment stating that "nothing is redistributed" and that only "identifiers plus locally computed values" are stored. ChEMBL's CC BY-SA 3.0 requires attribution and share-alike; the repo offers neither, and no attribution section exists.

Below those, three genuine claim-to-artefact mismatches: "paired t-test p = 0.978" is the Holm-adjusted value where the test gives 0.489 (I reproduced 0.48925 to five decimals) — and it runs in the direction that flatters a null acceptance; "contact counts swinging 13→52" appears nowhere in data/study_prodigy.json, whose actual range is 20→52, with an exhaustive search over all 63 subsets of the contact-type fields finding no series matching 13→52; and "%NIS 41.2–43.2%" excludes the true minimum of 40.83%. The badge row is stale on two counts (91 violations where the linked tool emits 124; 7 studies where 8 are registered), and data/validation_gate.json — the only committed gate artefact — is frozen at the superseded 91/11.

Net: the science holds, the presentation layer has drifted, and one gate metric is produced by a bug. Fix RI-01 through RI-03 before treating this README as a citable public record; RI-04 through RI-06 are quick corrections that should ship with them.

findings.title: Threshold indicators of exactly 0.0/1.0 are fed into Holm and published as "p_holm"; the practice is disclosed only in one code comment
findings.reproduction: grep -rn "p1 = \|p2 = \|p3 = " --include="*.py" platform/  &&  .venv/bin/python /private/tmp/.../scratchpad/v4.py  (prints p_raw/p_holm/verdicts for every data/study_*.json)  &&  grep -rn "threshold comparison\|not tests" --include="*.py" --include="*.md" platform/ README.md
findings.observed: 17 of the 24 hypothesis p-values across the 8 analysis modules are literals `0.0 if <threshold> else 1.0`. Published result files carry e.g. study_affinity_corrected.json p_holm {'H1':1.0,'H2':1.0,'H3':0.0}; study_candidate_screen.json {…,'H3_candidates_in_failed_band':0.0}; study_msa_specificity.json {…,'H3_msa_raises_natives':0.0}; study_prodigy.json {'H1':0.0,'H2':0.0,'H3':1.0}; study_peptide_interface.json {'H1':0.0,'H2':3e-05,'H3':0.0}. The disclosure grep returns exactly one line: platform/cbc/variance_analysis.py:123 "# H1 and H2 are threshold comparisons, not tests; they carry p = 0 or 1 by construction". Nothing in README.md or in any data/study_*.json says so. `p_raw` is emitted by only 2 of 8 modules (grep -n "p_raw" platform/studies/*.py platform/cbc/*.py → ache_affinity_benchmark.py:248, variance_analysis.py:170).
findings.why_wrong: p = 0.0 and p = 1.0 are not attainable p-values; they are indicator variables. Holm's step-down procedure is only defined on p-values that are (super-)uniform under their nulls, so applying it here has no error-control meaning. Worse, publishing the result under the key `p_holm` with no `p_raw` alongside makes it impossible for a reader of 6 of the 8 result files to see that the input was a threshold flag rather than a test. "Holm p = 0.0" printed by the console reporters (e.g. pose_analysis.py:275) reads as an infinitely significant test.
findings.fix: Stop putting indicators into the Holm family. Emit them as a separate `decision_flags` block (values TRUE/FALSE, not 0.0/1.0), run Holm only over the members that are genuine tests with K set to that count, and always emit `p_raw` next to `p_holm` in every result file. Set test_type="none" in the prespec for studies with no real test. At minimum, replicate variance_analysis.py:123's disclosure into README.md and into each report JSON.

findings.title: Study #7: the study's only real p-value receives NO multiplicity penalty because two indicator zeros occupy the top Holm ranks — yet it is published as "p_holm"
findings.reproduction: .venv/bin/python -c "import json;from scipy import stats;p=json.load(open('data/study_peptide_interface.json'));ok=[r for r in p['rows'] if r.get('ok')];pair=[(r['iptm'],r['dockq']) for r in ok if r.get('iptm') is not None];rr=stats.spearmanr([x for x,_ in pair],[y for _,y in pair]);print('n',len(pair),'rho',rr.statistic,'raw p',rr.pvalue);print('repo p_holm H2 =',p['analysis']['p_holm']['H2_iptm_calibration']);print('ratio applied =',p['analysis']['p_holm']['H2_iptm_calibration']/rr.pvalue);print('honest 3-test Holm =',3*rr.pvalue)"
findings.observed: n 16 rho 0.8470588 raw p 3.4680...e-05 / repo p_holm H2 = 3e-05 / ratio applied = 0.865 / honest 3-test Holm = 0.000104. README.md:366: "ipTM is well calibrated for this task — Spearman ρ = 0.847, p = 3×10⁻⁵." The registered analysis_plan (peptide_interface.py:127-128) says "Holm across the three hypotheses."
findings.why_wrong: H1 and H3 are indicators that evaluate to exactly 0.0, so they take Holm ranks 0 and 1 and the only genuine test (Spearman ipTM vs DockQ) is left at rank 2 with multiplier 1. The number published under the key `p_holm` is therefore the *unadjusted* p, rounded. A reader who takes the plan at its word ("Holm across the three hypotheses") will believe a multiplicity penalty was applied when none was. The correct Holm-adjusted value over a 3-member family is 1.04e-4, and over an honest 1-member family it is 3.47e-5 — but neither is what "p_holm = 3e-05" communicates. Rounding to 5 decimals also destroys the leading digit (3.468e-05 → 3e-05).
findings.fix: Run Holm over the genuine tests only (here K=1) and label the field `spearman_p_unadjusted`; or keep K=3 and report 1.04e-4. Round p-values to significant figures, not to 5 decimal places. State in README.md:366 whether the quoted p is adjusted.

findings.why_wrong: The pre-registered `discrimination_ratio` divides the SD of three group MEANS by the SD of INDIVIDUAL observations (prodigy_falsification.py:216-219). Those are not on the same footing: averaging 5 seeds shrinks the noise on each mean by √5, so the ratio is biased low by construction and cannot be read as signal:noise. The correct comparison (an F-test, or between-SD vs SE-of-mean = 1.0377/√5 = 0.464, ratio 3.04) rejects "no discrimination" at p = 0.0037. BasalSuper-AChE-TrkA-B5's five values are disjoint from the other two candidates' ten. The registered threshold makes the VERDICT defensible as a pre-specified decision rule, but the README's unqualified prose claim is false for the data. Note also that even on the ratio's own terms 1.36 > 1, so "not better than reseeding" does not follow.
findings.fix: Either report the F-test alongside (F(2,12)=9.23, p=0.0037) and rewrite README.md:274-277 to "a single PRODIGY run cannot rank these peptides — between-candidate SD 1.41 against single-run seed noise 1.04 — although the candidate means do differ (ANOVA p=0.004)"; or redefine the ratio as between-SD / SE-of-mean and re-register.

findings.title: prespec.verify_result never flags a pre-registered metric that was not computed, so a published report asserts "All pre-specified analyses were carried out as planned" when one was not

findings.observed: inference-variance-v1 True ['per_residue_plddt_sd'] ; pose-accuracy-v1 False ['posebusters_pass_rate'] ; others clean. data/study_inference_variance_analysis.json therefore ships prespec_audit = {"deviations": [], "confirmatory": true, "note": "All pre-specified analyses were carried out as planned."} while the pre-registered secondary metric per_residue_plddt_sd is null. findings.why_wrong: verify_result computes only `extra = reported - planned` (prespec.py:242). It also means README.md:316's claim that PoseBusters is a "declared deviation" is not backed by the automated record it points to.
findings.fix: In verify_result add: `missing = planned - reported` and `nulls = {k for k in planned & reported if result['metrics'][k] is None}`; append a deviation for each ("pre-specified metric X was not computed"). Re-run all eight analyses so the stored audits are regenerated.

findings.title: Two hypotheses are "confirmed" by failing to reject, and Holm is applied to them — which makes the acceptance strictly easier, the wrong direction
findings.reproduction: sed -n '138,146p' platform/studies/inference_variance.py  &&  .venv/bin/python -c "import json;a=json.load(open('data/study_inference_variance_analysis.json'));print('raw',a['p_raw']['H3_msa_immaterial_for_designed_sequences'],'-> holm',a['p_holm']['H3_msa_immaterial_for_designed_sequences'],'verdict',a['verdicts']['H3_msa_immaterial_for_designed_sequences'])"
findings.observed: confirmed_if=("|mean(with MSA) - mean(without MSA)| < the pooled across-seed SD from H1, and the paired t-test across candidates does not reject at Holm-adjusted 0.05"); falsified_if=("... or the paired t-test rejects at Holm-adjusted 0.05"). Output: raw 0.48924736813491787 -> holm 0.97849 verdict CONFIRMED. variance_analysis.py:138 gates on `adj[2] >= 0.05`. Underlying data: 4 of the 6 paired differences are exactly 0.0 (diffs*100 = [0.0, -0.5215, 0.0, 0.0, 2.5048, 0.0]).
findings.why_wrong: Holm only ever increases a p-value. When "confirmed" means p ≥ α, applying Holm makes confirmation strictly easier — a multiplicity correction used anti-conservatively. Separately, a non-significant t-test on 6 pairs, 4 of which are identically zero, is a statement about power, not about equivalence; the study has essentially no ability to detect a shift. The same shape appears in ache_affinity_benchmark H3 ("confirmed if |z| ≤ 2"), where p_holm = 0.81407 is printed next to the hypothesis but plays no role in the verdict (the verdict uses |z| only), which is misleading reporting.
findings.fix: For equivalence-style hypotheses use TOST against the stated margin (here the pooled across-seed SD) and Holm-adjust the TOST p, which then correctly makes equivalence HARDER to claim under multiplicity. Report the achieved power / the margin the design could actually exclude. For ache H3, either drop p3 from the Holm family or make the verdict depend on it.

findings.title: prespec reachability check: BH is accepted without the multiplicity multiplier, so an unreachable BH plan registers successfully
findings.reproduction: .venv/bin/python -c "import sys;sys.path.insert(0,'platform');from cbc import prespec as ps;H=(ps.Hypothesis('A','s','p1','c','f'),ps.Hypothesis('B','s','p2','c','f'));s=ps.Prespecification(study_id='x',question='q',primary_metric='m',primary_metric_justification='j',decision_threshold='d',n_planned=10,n_comparisons=20,multiplicity_correction='bh',alpha=0.05,stopping_rule='s',analysis_plan='a',hypotheses=H,test_type='permutation',n_permutations=100);print('returned',s.min_attainable_p());print('true BH floor',(1/101)*20);print('check()',s.check())"
findings.observed: returned 0.009900990099009901 / true BH floor 0.19801980198019803 / check() []  — i.e. registrable. register() also succeeded and stored "min_attainable_p": 0.009901.
findings.why_wrong: `multiplicity_correction` is typed Literal["none","bonferroni","holm","bh"] (prespec.py:79) but line 135 multiplies by K only for bonferroni and holm. Under Benjamini–Hochberg the most significant test's adjusted value is also p₍₁₎·K/1, so the floor is identical to Bonferroni's. The function under-reports it by a factor of K, and the UNREACHABLE VERDICT guard therefore never fires for a BH plan. No currently registered study uses BH, so nothing published is affected — this is a latent hole in the module the README advertises as the reachability guarantee.
findings.fix: Change prespec.py:135 to `if self.multiplicity_correction in ("bonferroni", "holm", "bh"):` and update the docstring at :124-125, which mentions only Bonferroni and Holm.

findings.title: prespec reachability check is off by one at the boundary: pmin == alpha registers, contradicting the module's own _n_needed()
findings.reproduction: .venv/bin/python -c "import sys;sys.path.insert(0,'platform');from cbc import prespec as ps;H=(ps.Hypothesis('A','s','p1','c','f'),ps.Hypothesis('B','s','p2','c','f'));s=ps.Prespecification(study_id='x',question='q',primary_metric='m',primary_metric_justification='j',decision_threshold='d',n_planned=10,n_comparisons=20,multiplicity_correction='holm',alpha=0.05,stopping_rule='s',analysis_plan='a',hypotheses=H,test_type='permutation',n_permutations=399);print('min_attainable_p',s.min_attainable_p());print('check()',s.check());print('_n_needed()',s._n_needed())"
findings.observed: min_attainable_p 0.05 / check() [] / _n_needed() 400
findings.why_wrong: Every study's decision rule is stated as strict inequality ("Holm-adjusted p < 0.05", e.g. ache_affinity_benchmark.py:90). With min_attainable_p exactly equal to alpha the test can never fire, which is precisely the defect the check exists to catch — yet `pmin > self.alpha` lets it through. The module is internally inconsistent: it accepts B=399 while its own `_n_needed()` says B must be ≥ 400. No registered study is affected (all declare test_type="parametric", raw_min = 0).
findings.fix: Change prespec.py:150 to `if pmin >= self.alpha:` and adjust the message text accordingly. Add a regression test asserting check() is non-empty at B = _n_needed() - 1 and empty at B = _n_needed().

findings.title: All eight prespecs declare test_type="parametric" when six of them run no parametric test, making every stored min_attainable_p vacuously 0.0
findings.reproduction: grep -h "test_type\|min_attainable_p\|study_id" prespec/*.json
findings.observed: All eight files show "min_attainable_p": 0.0 and "test_type": "parametric". Yet candidate-screen, affinity-corrected, pose-accuracy and prodigy-discrimination contain no test at all (all six/nine hypothesis p-values are `0.0 if <threshold> else 1.0` — see STAT-02), and msa-specificity/peptide-interface contain one each.
findings.why_wrong: prespec.py:132-133 assigns raw_min = 0.0 for anything that is not "permutation" or "exact", so declaring "parametric" makes the UNREACHABLE VERDICT check unconditionally pass. The reachability guarantee — the module's headline feature and the subject of its 15-line docstring — is therefore vacuous for every study in the repository, including the four that have no test to be reachable. The correct declaration for a threshold-decision study is test_type="none".
findings.fix: Set test_type="none" for the studies whose hypotheses are threshold decisions, set n_comparisons to the number of genuine tests, and re-register (the hashes will change, which is the intended visible consequence). Add a check() rule: if test_type=="none" and multiplicity_correction!="none", flag it, since there is nothing to correct.

findings.title: Study #11's "nis_variance_fraction" is a fraction of a sum of standard deviations, not a variance decomposition
findings.location: platform/studies/prodigy_falsification.py:224-229; published as metrics.nis_variance_fraction in data/study_prodigy.json; quoted at README.md:284
findings.reproduction: .venv/bin/python -c "import json,statistics,collections;p=json.load(open('data/study_prodigy.json'));ok=[r for r in p['rows'] if r.get('ok')];by=collections.defaultdict(list);[by[r['code']].append(r) for r in ok];C={'ic_cc':-0.09459,'ic_ca':-0.10007,'ic_pp':0.19577,'ic_pa':-0.22671,'nis_apolar':0.18681,'nis_charged':0.13810};c={k:statistics.stdev([statistics.fmean(x[k] for x in rs)*v for rs in by.values()]) for k,v in C.items()};print(c);print('sum of SDs',sum(c.values()));print('actual between-candidate SD of dG',statistics.stdev([statistics.fmean(x['dg'] for x in rs) for rs in by.values()]))"
findings.observed: contrib {'ic_cc': 0.1863, 'ic_ca': 0.5533, 'ic_pp': 0.1196, 'ic_pa': 0.7752, 'nis_apolar': 0.1279, 'nis_charged': 0.0663}; sum of SDs 1.8287; actual between-candidate SD of dG 1.4098. Reported nis_variance_fraction 0.1062 reproduces exactly, and README.md:284 reads "accounts for only 10.6% of the between-candidate variance".
findings.why_wrong: The denominator is a sum of standard deviations of signed terms (1.8287), which is not the total variance and does not equal the between-candidate SD it purports to decompose (1.4098) — the terms are correlated and signed, so SDs do not add. Calling the resulting share a "variance fraction" and quoting it as "10.6% of the between-candidate variance" attributes a decomposition property the quantity does not have. n = 3 groups also makes each stdev() a 2-df estimate.
findings.fix: Either compute a genuine decomposition — regress the per-candidate mean ΔG on the six term contributions and report partial R², or report Var(term)/Var(ΔG) with the covariance terms shown — or rename the metric `nis_share_of_summed_term_sds` and change README.md:284 to match. Re-registration is needed since the metric name is in the prespec.

findings.title: Huperzine A's z-score is computed against a reference mean/SD that includes Huperzine A itself
findings.reproduction: .venv/bin/python -c "import json,numpy as np;q=json.load(open('data/study_ache_affinity.json'));ok=[r for r in q['rows'] if r.get('ok')];err=np.abs(np.array([r['pred_pic50'] for r in ok])-np.array([r['meas_pic50'] for r in ok]));i=[j for j,r in enumerate(ok) if 'HUPERZINE' in r['name'].upper()][0];he=err[i];o=np.delete(err,i);print('self-inclusive z',(he-err.mean())/err.std(ddof=1),'repo',q['analysis']['huperzine_z']);print('leave-one-out z',(he-o.mean())/o.std(ddof=1))"
findings.observed: self-inclusive z 0.9400 repo 0.94 / leave-one-out z 1.0050
findings.why_wrong: H3 is "the disputed Huperzine result is representative", confirmed_if |z| ≤ 2. Including the tested point in the reference mean and SD shrinks |z| toward 0, which biases the test in favour of the hypothesis being confirmed. The correct statistic for "is this observation an outlier in this set" is a leave-one-out z (or Grubbs' test). Here the verdict is unchanged (0.94 vs 1.005, both well under 2), so no published conclusion moves.
findings.fix: Compute z against the other 14 errors: `o = np.delete(err, i); z = (hup_err - o.mean()) / o.std(ddof=1)`. Or use scipy's Grubbs-equivalent critical value for n=15. Note the change in the report so the prespec audit records it.

findings.title: Study #8's H2 compares two Spearman correlations against a hardcoded constant with no standard error
findings.reproduction: .venv/bin/python -c "import json;from scipy import stats;import numpy as np;q=json.load(open('data/study_affinity_corrected.json'));ok=[r for r in q['rows'] if r.get('corrected')];print('n',len(ok));print('rho',stats.spearmanr([r['pred_pic50'] for r in ok],[r['meas_pic50_corrected'] for r in ok]).statistic);print('repo delta_rho',q['analysis']['metrics']['delta_rho'],'vs hardcoded rho_v1',q['analysis']['metrics']['rho_v1'])" && grep -n 'rho_v1 = 0.304' platform/studies/affinity_corrected.py
findings.observed: n 14 / rho 0.19116... / repo delta_rho -0.1128 vs hardcoded rho_v1 0.304 / affinity_corrected.py:195:    rho_v1 = 0.304
findings.why_wrong: H2 ("the reference fix matters") is decided by `delta = rho - 0.304 > 0.15`. rho_v1 is a literal, so it carries no uncertainty and will silently go stale if study #1 is ever re-run (study #1's actual rho is 0.3036 on n=15, this study's is on n=14 — overlapping but not identical sets). Comparing two dependent correlations on n≈15 without a standard error means a 0.15 threshold is far inside the noise: this study's own bootstrap CI for rho is [−0.4622, 0.7303], width 1.19. The verdict (FALSIFIED, rho went down) happens to be robust to this, but the design could not have distinguished a real 0.15 improvement from noise.

State in known_confounds that at n=14 the design cannot resolve a 0.15 shift.

findings.title: The Wilson interval is implemented twice, verbatim, in two modules
findings.reproduction: grep -rn "def _wilson" --include="*.py" platform/
findings.observed: platform/cbc/pose_analysis.py:29:def _wilson(k: int, n: int, z: float = 1.96) ... ; platform/studies/peptide_interface.py:269:def _wilson(k: int, n: int, z: float = 1.96) ... — identical bodies, only local variable names differ (centre/half vs c/h). The pose_analysis copy carries the explanatory docstring; the peptide_interface copy has none.
findings.why_wrong: Two copies of a statistical primitive will drift. Both are currently correct (verified against the closed form and the standard k=81/n=263 example), so nothing published is wrong; this is maintenance risk only. Both also use z = 1.96 rather than 1.959964, which costs up to 1e-5 on an interval endpoint — immaterial at these n but inconsistent with a repo that reports 4 decimal places.
findings.fix: Move `_wilson` into a shared module (platform/cbc/stats.py, which does not currently exist) and import it in both places; default z to `scipy.stats.norm.isf(alpha/2)` so the coverage level is explicit rather than hardcoded.

unverified_concerns: Whether the 4-of-6 bit-identical with/without-MSA folds in the inference-variance study reflect a genuine empty MSA (the README's reading, plausible for designed sequences with no homologues) or a plumbing bug that silently dropped the --use_msa_server flag. I could not re-run Boltz to distinguish these, and the stored rows record no MSA depth or hit count. Study #10 found the MSA raises ipTM by +0.219 on the same candidate family, which sits uneasily beside a 0.33-pLDDT-unit shift with four exact zeros. Recording the returned MSA depth per fold would settle it.

Whether the pre-cutoff/post-cutoff split in study #7 and the recall/congeneric split in study #6 are actually leakage-free. The prespec's own known_confounds says Boltz's training split is not published, so deposition date is a proxy. I verified the arithmetic on the strata, not the strata themselves.

The DockQ chain-mapping deviation recorded in study #7's audit (explicit mapping raises KeyError, auto-search used instead) is a change to the scoring procedure made after seeing failures. It is disclosed and justified with a measured example (4XHV: explicit=KeyError, auto=0.899), but I did not re-run DockQ under either mapping to confirm the two agree on the other 15 complexes.
I checked the local README.md only. I did not fetch github.com/hopejsh/CognitionBioChem, so I cannot confirm the public page carries the same text at the same line numbers.

I did not re-execute any study's analyse() end-to-end (that would overwrite data/study_*.json); every number above was recomputed independently from the stored raw rows with scipy/numpy rather than by re-running the repo's own code path.
what_is_sound: The Holm loop is CORRECT in all eight implementations and there is no off-by-one. Every copy uses `running = max(running, (K - rank) * p_sorted)` with `rank` 0-indexed, which is exactly the (K - rank_1indexed + 1) multiplier, enforces monotonicity via the running max, and caps at 1.0. Verified by independent recomputation: ache-affinity raw (0.27136, 0.79316, 0.34724) -> Holm (0.81407, 0.81407, 0.81407), matching data/study_ache_affinity.json exactly; msa-specificity raw (0.76814, 1.0, 0.0) -> (1.0, 1.0, 0.0), matching.

The Wilson interval (pose_analysis.py:29-37) is correct. It matches the closed form at z=1.959964 to within 1e-5 at every k/n I tried, and reproduces the standard textbook example k=81, n=263 -> [0.25529, 0.36621]. The two published intervals reproduce exactly: recall 3/6 -> [0.1876, 0.8124], congeneric 2/6 -> [0.0968, 0.7000]. The n==0 guard returning (0,1) is the right degenerate behaviour.

The Fisher exact implementation (pose_analysis.py:40-51) is correct. Zero mismatches against scipy.stats.fisher_exact across 400 random 2x2 tables with entries 0-12 (tolerance 1e-9). The two-sided rule (sum all hypergeometric probabilities <= observed, with a 1+1e-9 relative tolerance for floating-point ties) is the same convention scipy uses. On the study's actual table [[3,3],[2,4]] both give p = 1.0, matching the published 1.0 and README.md:327-328.

The bootstrap is correctly specified and fully reproducible. `np.random.default_rng(0)` fixes the seed; `rng.integers(0, n, n)` draws indices with replacement and both arrays are indexed by the SAME draw, so pairing is preserved (this is the common bug and it is not present). The NaN filter is not biasing anything: I re-ran both bootstraps and 0 of 10000 resamples produced NaN in each. Both CIs reproduce to 4 decimals -- ache-affinity [-0.3285, 0.7658] and affinity-corrected [-0.4622, 0.7303].

The variance pooling is right and the docstring's reasoning is right. pooled_sd (variance_analysis.py:37-49) computes sqrt(mean of per-candidate sample variances) = 2.6615 pLDDT units, matching the published across_seed_sd_complex_plddt exactly. Because every candidate has exactly n=5 folds, this coincides to the last digit with the df-weighted pooled SD (also 2.6615), so the unweighted mean of variances is the correct estimator here. The docstring's warning is quantitatively vindicated: the SD of the pooled values is 15.7429, six times larger, because it absorbs between-candidate signal.

The core of prespec.min_attainable_p is correct: the raw floor 1/(B+1) for permutation tests and 1/(n+1) for exact tests, multiplied by K for the most significant comparison under Holm -- Holm's first step does multiply by K, so this is the right floor, not a Bonferroni approximation. The docstring's worked example reproduces exactly (K=20, exact test at n=41 -> 0.476190). The 1/(n+1) stand-in for exact tests errs conservatively (it overstates the floor), which is the safe direction. _n_needed() is also correct at the integer boundary: B=400 gives 0.049875 (reachable), B=399 gives 0.050000 (not).

Every headline correlation in the README states its n, either inline or in the sentence introducing the section: rho=0.304 with 'n = 15 of 17 planned' (README.md:163,172); rho=0.191 with 'The same 14 predictions' (README.md:380,387); rho=0.847 with '16 peptide-receptor X-ray complexes' (README.md:355,366); Fisher p and Wilson intervals with 'At n = 6 per stratum' (README.md:328). I looked for a naked correlation and did not find one.

Every point statistic I re-derived reproduces exactly under scipy/numpy from the stored raw rows -- Spearman rho and p and Pearson and Kendall for two affinity studies, the Spearman for peptide-interface (rho 0.847059, p 3.468e-05), the paired t for both t-test studies, the pose-accuracy fractions (0.4167 within 2A, median 3.943, mean 4.917, premium 0.1667), the peptide ipTM band confusion matrix (9/1/0/4/1/1), and all five prodigy metrics (between 1.4098, within 1.0377, ratio 1.359, range 2.4434, nis 0.1062). There is no arithmetic error anywhere in the reported numbers; the defects above are all definitional or presentational.

The study designs disclose their own power limits in advance rather than after the fact -- the 1/(N+1) empirical-p floor at N=3 decoys (candidate_screen.py known_confounds), the same floor at N=10 in msa-specificity's primary_metric_justification (which explicitly cites the project's own unreachable-verdict rule as the reason for pairing across candidates instead), and the n=5 seed caveat with its ~30% relative uncertainty on the SD. That is unusually disciplined and is the reason several of the findings above are presentational rather than substantive.
audits.verdict:
The arithmetic is clean; the statistical framing is not. I re-derived more than a dozen reported statistics independently with scipy and every single point estimate reproduces exactly -- Holm is implemented correctly in all eight copies (no (K-rank) off-by-one, monotonicity enforced, capped at 1), the Wilson interval matches the standard table, the Fisher exact matches scipy on 400 random tables, the bootstrap is correctly paired and seeded with zero NaNs dropped, and the variance pooling is the right pooling and coincides exactly with the df-weighted estimator because the design is balanced. Those five specific things the brief asked me to check are sound.

The problems are all one level up. Seventeen of the twenty-four hypothesis "p-values" are literals of the form `0.0 if threshold else 1.0`, they are fed into Holm, and the output is published under the key `p_holm` -- with `p_raw` emitted by only two of the eight modules, and the practice disclosed nowhere except a single code comment in one module. This is not merely cosmetic: in study #7 the two indicator zeros take the top two Holm ranks, so the study's ONLY genuine test (Spearman ipTM vs DockQ) receives no multiplicity penalty at all, and its raw p is published as "p_holm = 3e-05" under a plan that promises "Holm across the three hypotheses". Two other hypotheses are "confirmed" by failing to reject, and Holm is applied to those too -- which makes acceptance strictly easier, the wrong direction for a correction that only inflates p.

Three substantive results need correcting. README.md:229 states "paired t-test p = 0.978" when the paired t-test p is 0.489 (0.978 is the Holm value) -- a false statistic in the public face, in the self-serving direction. Study #10's paired t-test counts one molecule twice (HippoAChE-AlkaPept-X2 and BasalAChE-GorgeBlock-B1 are byte-identical sequences, and they contribute the two largest positive differences); de-duplicating to the true n=5 flips the published primary metric from +0.019 to -0.011. And study #11's claim that PRODIGY "does not distinguish different peptides better than reseeding" is contradicted by a one-way ANOVA on the same 15 values at p=0.0037, because the pre-registered discrimination ratio divides an SD of group means by an SD of individual observations.

Finally, the prespec module's advertised guarantees are weaker than claimed: verify_result never checks for pre-registered metrics that came back null, so data/study_inference_variance_analysis.json publishes "All pre-specified analyses were carried out as planned" while per_residue_plddt_sd was never computed; the unreachable-verdict check is off by one at pmin == alpha (contradicting its own _n_needed) and omits the K multiplier for BH; and because all eight studies declare test_type="parametric", every stored min_attainable_p is 0.0 and the reachability check is vacuous throughout.

None of this makes the studies' conclusions wrong -- all seven verdicts survive every correction I applied, and the project's negative results remain negative. The fixes are disclosure, relabelling, de-duplication, and about twenty lines in prespec.py. But the repository is public and its whole claim is methodological rigour, so shipping "Holm p = 0.0" in five result files and a mislabelled t-test p in the README is exactly the kind of thing it was rebuilt to stop doing.

findings.reproduction: .venv/bin/python /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-seunghojung-Documents-DeepMind-Bio/353ad1f9-0130-417c-ac3a-20b4832cf1f4/scratchpad/t_physics2.py  — builds two mmCIF files containing exactly two carbon atoms 1.0 A apart (a 2.4 A van der Waals interpenetration), identical except that one omits the optional _atom_site.type_symbol column, then calls physics.validate() on each.
findings.observed:
=== B: mmCIF with no type_symbol column -> clash detection silently disabled ===
  atoms: 2 elements: ['', '']
  clashes: 0  severe: 0  clashscore: 0.0  band: clean
  physically_valid: True   warnings/skips: []

  clashes: 1 severe: 1 clashscore: 500.0 band: very poor valid: False
findings.why_wrong: find_clashes filters `[a for a in atoms if a.element and a.element != "H"]`, so atoms with an empty element string are removed from the neighbour search entirely, while validate() computes the denominator as `sum(1 for a in atoms if a.element != "H")`, which counts them. The numerator is therefore structurally zero and the denominator non-zero, yielding clashscore 0.0 rather than None. quality_band() then returns 'clean' and physically_valid returns True because severe_clashes is empty. Nothing is appended to checks_skipped and no warning is emitted, so the caller receives a plausible number (0.0) and a passing verdict for a structure that was never examined. This is the exact silent-failure shape the module was written to eliminate.
findings.fix: Two changes. (1) In physics._parse_cif and _parse_pdb, when type_symbol is absent or blank, infer the element from label_atom_id using the PDB convention (first alphabetic character, with a two-letter check against VDW keys) instead of storing ''. (2) In validate(), compute `heavy` with the same predicate find_clashes uses (`a.element and a.element != 'H'`), and if any parsed atom still has a blank element, set rep.clashscore = None and append to rep.checks_skipped a line naming how many atoms had no element, so physically_valid cannot be True on an unexamined file.

findings.location: platform/cbc/predictor.py:273-275 (seen-set keyed on (chain, seq_id)); platform/cbc/physics.py:285 and 326 (by_res keyed on (a.chain, a.resi))
findings.reproduction: .venv/bin/python /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-seunghojung-Documents-DeepMind-Bio/353ad1f9-0130-417c-ac3a-20b4832cf1f4/scratchpad/t_cif.py   (CASE 1)\n.venv/bin/python /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-seunghojung-Documents-DeepMind-Bio/353ad1f9-0130-417c-ac3a-20b4832cf1f4/scratchpad/t_physics3.py   (second section: an L-Ala at auth_seq_id 100 ins_code '.' and an achiral Gly at auth_seq_id 100 ins_code 'A')
findings.observed:
=== CASE 1: insertion codes (antibody CDR numbering 100, 100A, 100B) ===
  4 distinct residues written (100, 100A, 100B, 101). parser residues: 2 [('H', 100, 'ALA'), ('H', 101, 'ALA')]

=== insertion-code residue MIXING corrupts the chiral volume ===
  atoms: 7  distinct (chain,resi): 1
  ground truth: 0 D-amino acids (an L-Ala and an achiral Gly)
  check_chirality reports: [{'residue': 'A/GLY100', 'chiral_volume': -2.484, 'note': 'negative chiral volume: D-amino acid'}]
  validate(): n_residues = 1 (true 2)  physically_valid = False
findings.why_wrong: _atom_site.pdbx_PDB_ins_code is part of the residue identity in every deposited PDB/mmCIF entry that uses insertion codes — antibody CDR numbering (Kabat/Chothia) and chymotrypsin-convention protease numbering both rely on them. predictor.parse_mmcif dedupes CAs on (chain, seq_id) alone, so residues 100/100A/100B collapse to one: the residue count and the reported sequence are both wrong. physics.parse_all_atoms keeps all the atoms but buckets them by (chain, resi), so last-write-wins mixes atoms from different residues into one dictionary. In the demonstrated case the merged bucket takes N, CA, C from the Gly (written second, insertion code A) and CB from the Ala, and check_chirality computes a chiral volume of -2.484 across two residues 20 A apart, flagging a D-amino acid where none exists and setting physically_valid = False. posebench.fetch_structure downloads real RCSB mmCIFs, so this path is reachable by the pose benchmark, not just by synthetic input.
findings.fix: Make the residue key a 3-tuple. In predictor.parse_mmcif read `ins = f[idx['pdbx_PDB_ins_code']]` (normalising '.' and '?' to '') and key `seen` on (chain, seq_id, ins); add the code to Residue so the sequence and the count are right. In physics._parse_cif and _parse_pdb (column 26 for PDB) capture the insertion code onto Atom, and key by_res on (chain, resi, icode) in check_bonds, check_chirality and check_cis_peptides. findings.title: registry.residue_at() silently resolves the declared 'auth' convention — and any unknown string — as 'mature'
findings.reproduction: .venv/bin/python /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-seunghojung-Documents-DeepMind-Bio/353ad1f9-0130-417c-ac3a-20b4832cf1f4/scratchpad/t_registry.py
findings.observed:
-- residue_at() with convention='auth' (a declared Convention) --
  canonical  10: T
  mature     10: V
  auth       10: V  <- silently returns the MATURE residue
  garbage    10: V

-- convert() with auth --
  auth->canonical raises: RegistryError cannot convert auth -> canonical without a PDB alignment
findings.why_wrong: The line is `idx = position - 1 if convention == 'canonical' else position - 1 + self.mature_offset`, a two-way branch over a three-valued Literal. 'auth' is one of the three conventions the module's own docstring defines ('author numbering in a specific PDB entry, which may match neither'), and convert() correctly refuses to handle it — but residue_at() answers anyway with the mature residue. A caller checking an author-numbered annotation gets a confident, wrong single-letter answer instead of an exception. The whole module exists because 'nothing anywhere records which convention any number is in'; this is the one place that must not guess. check_annotation() only iterates ('canonical','mature') so the shipped data/target_registry.json is unaffected, which is why this is MINOR rather than MAJOR.
findings.fix: Replace the ternary with an explicit dispatch: canonical -> position-1; mature -> position-1+self.mature_offset; anything else -> `raise RegistryError(f"cannot resolve a residue under convention {convention!r} without a PDB alignment")`. Mirror the wording already used in convert() so the two functions refuse the same inputs.

findings.title: registry.convert(canonical -> mature) returns zero and negative positions for signal-peptide residues, and residue_at() then maps them back into range and returns a letter
findings.reproduction: .venv/bin/python /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-seunghojung-Documents-DeepMind-Bio/353ad1f9-0130-417c-ac3a-20b4832cf1f4/scratchpad/t_registry.py
findings.observed:
-- convert() produces NON-POSITIVE mature positions for signal-peptide residues --
  O00206 offset=23  canonical   1 -> mature  -22   residue_at(mature)='M'  true canonical residue='M'
  O00206 offset=23  canonical  23 -> mature    0   residue_at(mature)='P'  true canonical residue='P'
  O00206 offset=23  canonical  24 -> mature    1   residue_at(mature)='E'  true canonical residue='E'
findings.why_wrong: Mature numbering starts at 1 at the first residue after signal-peptide cleavage; positions 0 and below do not exist in that convention. convert() applies the offset arithmetically with no domain check, and residue_at() then adds the offset straight back, so the out-of-domain index lands inside the sequence and a plausible residue letter is returned for a meaningless position. A caller round-tripping a TLR4 (O00206) signal-peptide residue through the two functions gets a self-consistent answer that is not a mature position. Round-trip fidelity itself is exact — I verified 0 failures over all 16 cached targets and every position — so this is a domain-checking omission, not an arithmetic error.
findings.fix: In convert(), after computing the canonical->mature result, `if out < 1: raise RegistryError(f"canonical position {position} lies inside the signal peptide of {self.uniprot} (offset {self.mature_offset}); it has no mature-chain position")`. In residue_at(), reject position < 1 for both conventions before indexing.

findings.title: peptide.isoelectric_point() silently clamps to 14.00 when the bracket does not contain a root
findings.reproduction: .venv/bin/python /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-seunghojung-Documents-DeepMind-Bio/353ad1f9-0130-417c-ac3a-20b4832cf1f4/scratchpad/t_peptide2.py
findings.observed:
-- pI clamping at hi=14 (silent) --
  R*20   pI= 13.78  net_charge(pH=14)=  -0.387  net_charge(pI)= -0.0027
  R*40   pI= 14.00  net_charge(pH=14)=  +0.226  net_charge(pI)= +0.2261
  R*60   pI= 14.00  net_charge(pH=14)=  +0.839  net_charge(pI)= +0.8392
  R*100  pI= 14.00  net_charge(pH=14)=  +2.065  net_charge(pI)= +2.0653
findings.why_wrong: The bisection runs on the fixed bracket [0, 14] and never checks that net_charge changes sign across it. For an arginine-rich peptide with more than ~33 arginines the charge is still positive at pH 14 (R pKa 12.5 gives +0.0307 per residue there, against -1.0 from the C-terminus), so every iteration sets lo = mid and the function returns exactly 14.00 — a value at which the peptide carries a net charge of +0.226, not zero. The return type is a float with no flag, so the caller cannot distinguish a converged pI from a clamp. Everything else in the function is correct: Gly and poly-Ala both give 6.10 = (8.6+3.6)/2, exactly consistent with the declared EMBOSS pKa set, and |net_charge(pI)| < 0.003 in every converged case.
findings.fix: Before bisecting, evaluate net_charge at both ends. If they share a sign, either widen the bracket (0 to 20 is enough for any natural sequence) or return None and add an entry to PeptideReport.warnings naming the residual charge at the bracket end. Do not return a number the function knows is not a root.

findings.title: thermo.check()'s over-precision warning fires only on values that are exact multiples of 0.1, so it stays silent on dG values reported to MORE decimal places
findings.reproduction: .venv/bin/python /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-seunghojung-Documents-DeepMind-Bio/353ad1f9-0130-417c-ac3a-20b4832cf1f4/scratchpad/t_thermo2.py
findings.observed:
-- over-precision heuristic: which dG values get the 'no uncertainty' issue? --
  dG=-12.0      decimals=1  over-precision flagged: True
  dG=-12.3      decimals=1  over-precision flagged: True
  dG=-12.34     decimals=2  over-precision flagged: False
  dG=-12.345    decimals=3  over-precision flagged: False
  dG=-12.3456   decimals=4  over-precision flagged: False
  dG=-9.6       decimals=1  over-precision flagged: True
  dG=-9.65      decimals=2  over-precision flagged: False
findings.why_wrong: The guard is `if abs(dg * 10 - round(dg * 10)) < 1e-9`, which asks 'is dG an exact multiple of 0.1', not 'was dG reported without an uncertainty interval'. The message it emits — 'dG is reported to 0.1 kcal/mol with no uncertainty interval ... the best available method has ~1.1 kcal/mol RMSE' — is exactly as applicable, and more so, to -12.34 and -12.3456, yet those pass silently. The check therefore has an inverted sensitivity: the more over-precise the reported value, the less likely it is to be flagged. Because check() takes dG as a float it cannot recover the source precision at all.
findings.fix: Drop the multiple-of-0.1 test. Flag whenever a dG is supplied and no uncertainty was declared, e.g. add an `uncertainty_kcal: float | None = None` parameter to check() and emit the issue when it is None. If source-string precision is genuinely wanted, have parse_dg return the matched text alongside the float and count the decimal digits there, where the information exists.

findings.title: thermo.parse_kd() matches units case-insensitively but looks them up case-sensitively, silently returning None for common capitalisations, and accepts a bare 'm' as molar
findings.location: platform/cbc/thermo.py:106-113 (regex uses re.I; lookup at line 112 is `UNIT_TO_MOLAR.get(unit) or UNIT_TO_MOLAR.get(unit.replace('m','M'))`)
findings.reproduction: .venv/bin/python /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-seunghojung-Documents-DeepMind-Bio/353ad1f9-0130-417c-ac3a-20b4832cf1f4/scratchpad/t_thermo.py
findings.observed:
parse_kd cases:
    'Kd = 0.32 nM' -> (3.2000000000000003e-10, 'Kd = 0.32 nM')
    'Kd = 5 UM' -> (None, 'Kd = 5 UM')
    'Kd = 5 MM' -> (None, 'Kd = 5 MM')
    'KD = 7 Nm' -> (None, 'KD = 7 Nm')
    'Kd = 5 m' -> (5.0, 'Kd = 5 m')
    'Kd = 1.2e-9 M' -> (None, '')

(and) parse_kd('Kd = 5.5.5 nM') raised ValueError: could not convert string to float: '5.5.5'
findings.why_wrong: The regex carries re.I so it matches 'UM', 'MM' and 'Nm', but UNIT_TO_MOLAR is keyed on exact case and the only fallback is `unit.replace('m','M')`, which repairs 'nm'->'nM' but turns 'UM' into 'UM' and 'MM' into 'MM'. Those inputs return (None, matched_text): the caller sees 'no Kd found' for text that plainly contains one, and a downstream consistency check silently does not run. Separately, `Kd = 5 m` yields 5.0 M — a bare lowercase 'm' is not a concentration unit and should not produce a number. Scientific notation is not matched at all, and a malformed number raises an uncaught ValueError out of a function whose contract is to return None when it cannot parse.
findings.fix: Normalise before lookup: `factor = UNIT_TO_MOLAR.get(_CANON.get(unit.lower(), unit))` with an explicit lowercase map {'m':'M','mm':'mM','um':'uM','µm':'uM','μm':'uM','nm':'nM','pm':'pM','fm':'fM'}, and drop re.I from the unit group so a bare lowercase 'm' cannot match molar while 'mM' still can. Extend the number pattern to `[-+]?\\d*\\.?\\d+(?:[eE][-+]?\\d+)?` and wrap the float() in try/except returning (None, matched_text).

findings.reproduction: .venv/bin/python /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-seunghojung-Documents-DeepMind-Bio/353ad1f9-0130-417c-ac3a-20b4832cf1f4/scratchpad/t_stats.py

unverified_concerns: Multi-model mmCIF files: physics.parse_all_atoms ignores _atom_site.pdbx_PDB_model_num and merges every model. My CASE 3 in t_cif.py wrote 6 CA rows across 2 models and parse_all_atoms returned 6 atoms while predictor.parse_mmcif returned 3 residues. On an NMR ensemble, where models overlap in space, this would generate large numbers of spurious clashes and a meaningless clashscore. I could not reproduce actual harm because no multi-model file exists in the repository and posebench filters RCSB to X-ray only.

Alternate conformations: predictor.parse_mmcif takes the first CA per (chain, seq_id) with no occupancy check, so it silently prefers altloc A even when altloc B has the higher occupancy; physics.parse_all_atoms keeps both copies, which would make altloc A and altloc B of the same residue score as a clash against each other. My CASE 2 showed the parsers disagree (2 residues vs 3 atoms) but I could not find a real file in the repository that triggers it.

physics._parse_cif drops an entire atom when any parsed field is non-numeric: an atom whose B_iso_or_equiv is '?' vanished (CASE 5: 2 atoms written, 1 parsed), and an atom whose row splits into fewer whitespace tokens than there are columns (a quoted value containing a space) vanished from both parsers (CASE 6). The clash count, clashscore and residue count all silently shrink. I could not find a real file in this repository that contains either pattern, so I cannot show a wrong published number from it.

posebench._sequence_correspondence concatenates every chain into a single string before aligning. When the reference and the model list their chains in different orders, residues are lost: in my two-chain test (78-residue receptor + 15-residue peptide) 15 of 93 residues went unpaired purely from ordering. Critically they were LOST, never mispaired — the same-amino-acid guard held, and identity violations were 0 in every case I ran — so the failure degrades safely. The current pose study filters to single-protein-entity entries, so I could not show this affecting a published number; it would matter for the peptide-interface work.

I did not audit corpus.py, prespec.py, variance_analysis.py, compute/admet.py or compute/structure.py. I also did not re-run any Boltz prediction, per the brief, so all predictor findings rest on the archived artefacts in runs/ plus synthetic known-answer files.

physics.check_disulfides marks a sulfur as 'paired' whenever another SG is within SS_MAX = 3.0 A even if the S-S distance is far from the 2.05 +/- 0.03 ideal, so a badly modelled thiol pair is removed from free_cysteines while being reported with geometry_ok False. I confirmed the code path by reading it but constructed no failing case against real data.
what_is_sound: thermo.py dG<->Kd conversion is exact. kd_to_dg(1e-9) returned -12.278223119527329, bit-identical to the hand computation 1.987204259e-3*298.15*math.log(1e-9); dg_to_kd(-12.0) returned 1.5993332334903478e-09, identical to math.exp(-12/(R*T)); the round trip dg_to_kd(kd_to_dg(1e-9)) gave 1.0000000000000007e-09. RT = 0.59248494982085 as documented.

thermo.check() consistency arithmetic is right: a stated dG of -18.4 against Kd = 1 nM produced discrepancy_kcal 6.122 and discrepancy_orders 4.487, matching the independent abs(log10(1e-9/dg_to_kd(-18.4))) = 4.487. Degenerate input is handled by raising, not by returning a number: kd = 0.0 and kd = -1e-9 both raised ValueError out of math.log. The REFERENCE_AFFINITIES table is internally consistent — -18.3 kcal/mol maps to 38.5 fM (biotin-streptavidin), -12.3 to 964 pM against a label reading 'Kd ~ 1 nM', -9.6 to 91.9 nM against 'Kd ~ 100 nM', -6.8 to 10.4 uM against 'Kd ~ 10 uM'.

peptide.py molecular weight is correct against two independent calculations. The RESIDUE_MASS table agrees with RDKit free-amino-acid MW minus water to a worst case of 0.0074 Da over all 20 residues. Whole-peptide MW: angiotensin II cbc 1046.19 vs RDKit-independent 1046.20 (+0.007) vs Biopython 1046.18; insulin B chain cbc 3399.93 vs 3399.96 (+0.026) vs Biopython 3399.89; the 36-mer from runs/0083b1c7d3e6 cbc 4316.87 vs 4316.92 (+0.050). My initial memory-based reference for insulin B chain was wrong and the module was right.

peptide.py GRAVY is exact: -0.325 / -1.044 / +0.303 for angiotensin II, bradykinin and insulin B chain, identical to Biopython to three decimals, and matching my hand sum (-3.5-4.5+4.2-1.3+4.5-3.2-1.6+2.8)/8 = -0.325.

peptide.net_charge is a correct Henderson-Hasselbalch sum: for a single Lys at pH 7.4 the module returned 0.9404095723572898 against my hand value 0.9404. Isoelectric points are internally consistent with the declared EMBOSS pKa set — Gly and poly-Ala both give 6.10 = (8.6+3.6)/2 — and |net_charge(pI)| was below 0.003 in every converged case. The divergence from Biopython's pI (7.54 vs 6.74 for angiotensin II) is the documented Bjellqvist-versus-EMBOSS pKa difference, not an error.

physics.check_chirality has the correct sign, verified on real data rather than asserted. Across all 24 Boltz models in runs/ there are 1256 residues carrying N, CA, C and CB, and the D-amino-acid count is 0. Mirroring one model (x -> -x) flipped 35 of 35 testable residues to D. The reported inverted-sign bug is genuinely fixed.

physics.find_clashes' uniform-grid neighbour search misses nothing at cell boundaries. Against a brute-force all-pairs implementation on four real Boltz models the clash sets were identical (17/17, 20/20, 23/23, 14/14 with 0 missing and 0 extra). I then ran 20,000 randomized one-dimensional trials placing two carbons at uniformly random absolute positions across +/-60 A with separations spanning the 3.0 A limit, and 5,000 randomized three-dimensional trials with the largest vdW pair (I-I, limit 3.56 A): 0 mismatches in both. The 4.0 A cell exceeds the maximum possible clash distance, so the +/-1 cell stencil is provably sufficient.

physics.check_bonds correctly flags backbone outliers and is not confused by gaps in residue numbering: a file with residues numbered 1 and 3 and deliberately wrong geometry produced ('A/ALA1','N-CA',3.0,77.0 sigma), ('A/ALA1','CA-C',1.0,-25.0), and the same pair for ALA3.

predictor.parse_mmcif reads the repository's real Boltz output correctly. Over all 24 runs the residue count equals an independent count of distinct (auth_asym_id, auth_seq_id) CA rows, and for the 22 runs with an input.yaml the parsed one-letter sequence is character-for-character identical to the submitted sequence. Mean pLDDT matches the Boltz plddt .npz to two decimals on 23 of 24 runs; the 24th (919fef2194e3) is not a defect — that npz has 601 entries for 583 residues plus 18 ligand atoms, and the parser's 93.34 equals npz[:583].mean()*100 = 93.34 exactly, i.e. the documented separation of ligand atoms from the polymer is working.

predictor.band_fractions partitions the pLDDT scale without gaps or overlap: the probe [100, 90, 89.999, 70, 69.999, 50, 49.999, 0] gave exactly 0.25 in each of the four AlphaFold bands, summing to 1.0. low_confidence_regions honours min_len correctly, returning (0,2,3) and (5,8,4) and dropping a trailing 2-residue run.

posebench._sequence_correspondence is correct for every case the brief asked about, with zero residue-identity violations in all of them: identical sequences under offset author numbering (78/78 paired); a 10-residue disordered gap in the crystal (68/68); a 10-residue insertion in the model (78/78); a model truncated to 48 of 78 residues (48/48); a model with an internal 20-residue deletion (58/58); a 9-mer model against a 78-mer crystal (9/9); and ambiguous poly-alanine both equal-length and shorter (40/40, 20/20). Two unrelated sequences paired 1 residue, which is the safe outcome.

registry.py mature-offset derivation is right and is genuinely derived, not assumed. Across all 16 cached UniProt records the offset equals the CHAIN feature start minus one and equals the SIGNAL feature end wherever a signal peptide exists (14 of 16). The two apparent exceptions are correct behaviour: P29474/eNOS has no signal peptide but a CHAIN starting at 2 (initiator-Met removal), giving offset 1, and the no-signal targets correctly give offset 0.

registry.convert() round-trips exactly. Over all 16 cached targets and every position from 1 to the full sequence length, mature -> canonical -> mature returned the original position in every case: 0 failures.

pose_analysis.py statistics are correct. _fisher agrees with scipy.stats.fisher_exact (two-sided) to a worst absolute difference of 4.44e-16 over 400 random 2x2 tables, including the extremes (0,10,10,0) -> 1.08251e-05 and (20,0,0,20) -> 1.45089e-11. _wilson matches the closed-form Wilson score interval to six decimals at k=0, k=n and interior points, and returns (0.0, 1.0) rather than dividing by zero at n=0. The Holm step-down is a correct implementation: raw [0.01, 0.04, 0.03] gives [0.03, 0.06, 0.06], preserving monotonicity.

The published pose-accuracy numbers reproduce exactly from the stored per-entry RMSDs in data/study_pose_accuracy.json: fraction under 2 A 0.4167, median 3.943, mean 4.917, fraction under 5 A 0.5833, recall Wilson [0.1876, 0.8124], congeneric Wilson [0.0968, 0.700], interpolation premium 0.1667, and Fisher p 1.0 — the last confirmed independently by scipy. n_observed 12 equals the sum of the stratum counts.

All six verify_all.py suites pass with the documented expected exit codes, including the data gate that is designed to exit 1 on legacy data (124 violations across 13 categories). The gate failing is intentional and correctly reported as a PASS by the harness.
audits.verdict:
The core arithmetic of this platform is sound, and two things that were most at risk are demonstrably correct. The chirality sign fix is real: 0 D-amino acids across 1256 testable residues in all 24 Boltz models, flipping to 35/35 on a mirrored copy. The grid neighbour search misses nothing: identical to brute force on four real structures and 0 mismatches in 25,000 randomized boundary trials. Thermodynamic conversions, peptide MW, GRAVY and net charge, the mature-offset derivation, convert() round-tripping, Fisher, Wilson and Holm, and the published pose-accuracy statistics all reproduce against independent calculations. _sequence_correspondence handles gaps, insertions and shorter-than-crystal models with zero identity violations.

The defects that matter are all silent-failure paths rather than wrong formulas, and there are four. An mmCIF lacking the optional type_symbol column disables clash detection entirely and returns clashscore 0.0, band 'clean', physically_valid True for two carbons interpenetrating by 2.4 A, with nothing in checks_skipped. provenance.audit() does not descend into lists of numbers, lists of lists, or tuples, so its docstring claim to report 'every numeric leaf' is false — currently latent, since an exhaustive walker over dataset.json finds the same zero it does. predictor.load() silently degrades to source='mmcif_only' on the repository's own archived Boltz artefacts, dropping ptm, iptm and the whole PAE matrix because the archive renamed the files past its globs, which makes interface_pae() return None for all 24 runs. And insertion codes are ignored by both parsers, collapsing distinct residues and producing a false D-amino-acid call with physically_valid False on an L-Ala plus achiral Gly pair — reachable through posebench's RCSB downloads, not only synthetic input.

None of these has produced a wrong number in the shipped study data that I could find. Separately, the repository is now public with no LICENSE file among its 531 tracked files while the README asserts 'Private research', and the data-gate badge still reads 91 violations against the 124 the gate actually emits and the 124 the README body itself states. Fix NUM-01 through NUM-04 before anyone points these modules at a crystal structure, and fix NUM-14 before anyone tries to reuse the repository at all.

findings.title: Public repo has no LICENSE and redistributes 229 Apache-2.0 files copyrighted by Google LLC under a blanket "Private research © Seung H. Jung" notice
findings.location: README.md:569-574 (License section); repo root (LICENSE absent); .agents/skills/** (229 files); skills-lock.json:1-10
findings.reproduction: cd /Users/seunghojung/Documents/DeepMind_Bio && git ls-files | grep -icE '(^|/)(LICENSE|COPYING|NOTICE)' ; find .agents -iname 'LICENSE*' -o -iname 'NOTICE*' -o -iname 'COPYING*' | wc -l ; git ls-files | grep -c '^.agents/' ; head -8 .agents/skills/chembl-database/scripts/*.py ; head -8 skills-lock.json ; sed -n '569,575p' README.md
findings.observed: License/NOTICE file count in the whole tracked tree: `0`. LICENSE/NOTICE/COPYING inside .agents: `0`. Tracked files under .agents/: `229` (22,469 lines of Python, vs 12,077 lines of the project's own Python). Vendored file header: `# Copyright 2026 Google LLC` / `# Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 (the "License");` / `# You may obtain a copy of the License at` / `#     http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0`. skills-lock.json declares `"source": "google-deepmind/science-skills", "sourceType": "github"` for every skill. WebFetch of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google-deepmind/science-skills/main/LICENSE returns "Apache License, Version 2.0". README.md:571-574 reads: `Private research. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or connected to Google DeepMind or the AlphaFold team.` … `© 2026 Seung H. Jung`.
findings.why_wrong: Two independent legal defects on a now-public repo. (a) Apache-2.0 §4(a)/(d) requires a redistributor to give recipients a copy of the License and to retain attribution notices; the repo ships 229 Google-LLC-copyrighted Apache-2.0 files, keeps the per-file headers that point at a LICENSE that is not there, adds no NOTICE, and states no attribution in the README — while README's only licence statement asserts a proprietary, all-rights-reserved posture and a single personal copyright over the whole tree. That posture is not the author's to assert over Google's files. (b) The author's own 12,077 lines carry no licence at all, which under copyright default means all rights reserved: a third party who clones the public repo has no legal permission to copy, modify or run it, so the work is unreproducible as a matter of law before any technical question arises. The README's "not affiliated with Google DeepMind" disclaimer compounds rather than cures this, because the repo is in fact redistributing Google DeepMind code without saying so.
findings.fix: 1) Add a root LICENSE for the author's own code (MIT or Apache-2.0 — Apache-2.0 is the least friction given the vendored tree) and replace README §License with the SPDX identifier plus the existing trademark disclaimer. 2) Either remove .agents/skills/ from the repo (add `.agents/` to .gitignore and `git rm -r --cached .agents`, restoring it from skills-lock.json at setup time), or keep it and add: `.agents/skills/LICENSE` (a verbatim Apache-2.0 copy), a root `NOTICE` naming "Portions © 2026 Google LLC, from google-deepmind/science-skills, Apache-2.0", a THIRD_PARTY.md, and a README §Third-party code section. Removing it is preferable — it is 65% of the repo's Python and none of it is exercised by verify_all.py.

findings.title: The committed dataset and the public UI state "No structure prediction has been run in this repository", flatly contradicting the README's headline claim
findings.location: platform/build_dataset.py:206-207; data/dataset.json (disclosure.headline); index.html:25-33; app.js:115-118; contradicted by README.md:3-4 and README.md:18-19
findings.reproduction: cd /Users/seunghojung/Documents/DeepMind_Bio && git rev-parse --short HEAD && git show HEAD:data/dataset.json | ./.venv/bin/python -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print('git_sha:',d['git_sha']); print('HEADLINE:',d['disclosure']['headline'])" && grep -n 'disclosure' app.js && sed -n '25,33p' index.html && sed -n '3,4p;18,19p' README.md
findings.observed: HEAD = `c28b768`. Committed dataset: `git_sha: a514a1a` / `HEADLINE: No structure prediction has been run in this repository.` app.js:116 `setText('disclosure-headline', d.headline || '');` renders it. index.html:26-29 hardcodes the same string as the default, under the comment `<!-- The single most important element on the page. -->`. README.md:3-4: "It **runs real structure prediction**". README.md:18-19: "Structure prediction is **real**: Boltz-2 v2.2.1 (MIT) runs locally on Apple MPS and produced every structure in `runs/`." The accompanying detail string in the same dataset object reads "It does not itself run AlphaFold3 or any other predictor, and it contains no binding-affinity calculation."
findings.why_wrong: Both statements cannot be true, and runs/manifest.json settles it: 24 real Boltz-2 runs are content-addressed and committed, so the disclosure is the stale, false one. On a public repo the single element the page itself calls "the most important" tells every visitor the exact opposite of what the project actually did — and the detail string additionally denies the affinity computation that platform/cbc/compute/ and four studies depend on. verify_frontend.py passes on this, so no suite catches it. Because the repo's whole credibility rests on the retraction of an earlier fabrication, a stale disclosure that understates the work is as damaging as one that overstates it: a reader cannot tell which of the two contradictory public claims to trust.
findings.fix: Rewrite the disclosure in platform/build_dataset.py:206-215 to match reality ("Structure prediction is real: Boltz-2 2.2.1 produced the 24 artefacts in runs/ and the study folds; binding affinity is predicted but uncalibrated and is never rendered as a free energy"), update the hardcoded fallback at index.html:28-29 to the same text, regenerate data/dataset.json, and add an assertion to platform/verify_frontend.py that the disclosure headline in data/dataset.json equals the hardcoded fallback in index.html and does not contain the string "No structure prediction has been run".

findings.title: No dependency manifest anywhere: 12,077 lines of project Python with zero declared dependencies and zero pinned versions
findings.location: repo root (requirements.txt / pyproject.toml / lock file all absent); README.md:80-82
findings.reproduction: cd /Users/seunghojung/Documents/DeepMind_Bio && git ls-files | grep -Ei 'requirement|pyproject|setup\.py|setup\.cfg|Pipfile|poetry|\.lock|environment\.ya?ml|conda|\.toml|LICEN|COPYING|CITATION|Dockerfile|CONTRIBUTING|NOTICE' && git ls-files '*.py' | grep -v '^.agents/' | xargs grep -hoE '^[[:space:]]*(from|import) [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*' | awk '{print $2}' | sort -u && git grep -n 'biopython 1.84\|biopython 1.88' -- . | grep -v '^.agents'
findings.observed: The manifest grep returns only vendored third-party artefacts (36 `.agents/**/citation.bib` files and one `.agents/skills/alphagenome-single-variant-analysis/pyproject.toml`) — no root manifest of any kind. Third-party imports actually used by the project's own code: `Bio admet_ai certifi numpy prodigy_prot rdkit sascorer scipy`. README.md:81 declares only four: `pip install rdkit numpy scipy certifi`. Versions appear only as free prose inside research/review JSON, and they conflict: reviews/idea_panel.json:713 says "biopython 1.84/1.88" while research/algorithms.json:441 says "biopython 1.88". The actual environment, readable only from the local venv and not from the repo, is: Python 3.14.6 / rdkit 2026.3.5, numpy 2.5.2, scipy 1.18.0, biopython 1.88, admet_ai 2.0.1, prodigy-prot 2.4.0, posebusters 0.6.5, chemprop 2.3.1, torch 2.13.0, pandas 3.0.5; plus .venv312 (Python 3.12.14, boltz 2.2.1, numpy 1.26.4, scipy 1.13.1) and .venvdockq (dockq 2.1.3, numpy 1.26.4, biopython 1.88).
findings.why_wrong: A third party cannot reconstruct the environment from the repo alone. Three mutually incompatible environments are required (the main stack needs numpy>=2, Boltz pins numpy 1.26.4, DockQ 2.1.3 pins numpy<2), and nothing in version control says so in machine-readable form. The scientific results are version-sensitive by the project's own admission — reviews/idea_panel.json:3336 pins a SASA regression value to "biopython 1.88, ShrakeRupley n_points=960" precisely so "a library upgrade or a protocol drift fails loudly" — yet the version that guarantee depends on is recorded nowhere a tool can read, and is self-contradictory where it is recorded.
findings.fix: Add three pinned manifests at the root — requirements.txt (main: rdkit==2026.3.5, numpy==2.5.2, scipy==1.18.0, certifi==2026.7.22, biopython==1.88, admet-ai==2.0.1, prodigy-prot==2.4.0, posebusters==0.6.5), requirements-boltz.txt (boltz==2.2.1, numpy==1.26.4, scipy==1.13.1), requirements-dockq.txt (dockq==2.1.3, numpy==1.26.4, biopython==1.88) — plus a pyproject.toml with `requires-python = ">=3.14"` and a `uv.lock` or `pip freeze` lock per environment. Generate them from the live venvs (`./.venv/bin/pip freeze`) so the pins are the versions the published numbers were produced with, and delete the conflicting prose version claims or make them cite the manifest.
